title: Quantile bootstrap lab notes
content:
Context: quick exploratory runs to understand variance in p95/p99 estimates for short bursty workloads. Wanted a cheap way to get confidence intervals without running large long-duration sweeps.

Goal: use bootstrap resampling on 10 short trials to produce approximate 95% CIs for p95/p99 token latency and end-to-end request latency under three batching configs. Not a replacement for full stress testing — just signal.

Hypothesis: p99 will have wide bootstrap CI for small n=10, but relative ordering between configs should still be visible (A < B < C) if effect sizes are large.

Environment:
- Cluster: dev-gpu-pool-7 (mixed A10/NVIDIA T4), single-zone (us-west1).
- Model: distilled-ggml-small (256 context, quantized int8 variant).
- Workload: synthetic Poisson arrivals with mean QPS=45, bursts with lambda multiply x5 for 200ms every 3s. 60s trials.
- Client: wrk2-like driver, 8 concurrency, 128B prompt -> ~40 token responses.
- Metrics collected: per-request token-latency (server-side), end-to-end wall time, cpu/gpu util, KV cache hit flag.

Configs tested:
- cfgA: dynamic-batching enabled, max_batch=64, batch_timeout_ms=5
- cfgB: dynamic-batching enabled, max_batch=128, batch_timeout_ms=12
- cfgC: batching disabled (direct single-request execution)

Run plan:
- For each config: run 10 identical 60s trials (fresh server warm restart every trial to control warm-cache variance).
- Record raw per-request latencies (token and e2e). Persist CSVs to /tmp/quantile-bootstrap/<cfg>/run-<i>.csv
- Offline bootstrap: resample trials (sample with replacement at trial level) 1000 bootstrap reps; compute p95 and p99 across pooled requests in each bootstrap sample.

Quick commands used (local driver):
- ./benchdriver --qps 45 --duration 60 --pattern burst --concurrency 8 --out /tmp/quantile-bootstrap/cfgA/run-1.csv --cfg cfgA.yaml
- python tools/bootstraps.py --input-dir /tmp/quantile-bootstrap/cfgA --reps 1000 --metric token_latency_ms --quantiles 0.95,0.99 --output /tmp/quantile-bootstrap/summary-cfgA.json

Raw high-level numbers (median across 10 trials before bootstrap, token-latency ms):
- cfgA median p95 = 18.9 ms, p99 = 42.7 ms
- cfgB median p95 = 20.4 ms, p99 = 57.1 ms
- cfgC median p95 = 27.3 ms, p99 = 88.9 ms

Bootstrap 95% CI (approx) for token latency (values in ms):
- cfgA p95 CI: [16.1, 23.5], p99 CI: [34.0, 68.2]
- cfgB p95 CI: [17.8, 26.0], p99 CI: [41.2, 93.7]
- cfgC p95 CI: [23.0, 35.6], p99 CI: [70.4, 125.9]

Interpretation notes: (scratch)
- Ordering is preserved: cfgA < cfgB < cfgC for both quantiles by medians.
- p99 CIs are wide — especially for cfgC (no batching) where upper bounds blow out. This matches intuition: single-request execution has higher variance under bursts.
- cfgB has slightly higher median p99 than cfgA; CI overlap suggests difference might not be significant at 95% when only 10 trials.
- Bootstrapping at trial-level captured trial-to-trial variability (cache priming + cold-start spikes).

Micro-observations from logs:
- Many p99 events coincide with GPU context switch logs (timestamped) and a KV cache-miss followed by full attention recompute.
- When batch_timeout_ms increased (cfgB), we saw higher average batch sizes during steady state but also longer tail because a partial-batch occasionally waited and then executed large batches that caused scheduling jitter.
- cfgA's tighter timeout smoothed jitter at cost of slightly lower throughput efficiency.

ASCII plot (median p99 bootstrap distribution approximate sparkline per config):
- cfgA: ▁▂▃▅▅▆▇▆▅▃▁ (concentrated center, shorter tails)
- cfgB: ▂▃▅▆▇▇▇▅▃▂ (fatter upper tail)
- cfgC: ▁▂▂▃▅▇████ (long heavy tail to the right)

Things to check / next steps:
- Increase trial count to 30 for a follow-up where we suspect marginal differences (cfgA vs cfgB). 10 trials were cheap but borderline for p99 sensitivity.
- Instrument to capture per-request batch-size in traces (so we can correlate large-batch events with p99 spikes).
- Re-run with a larger model (512 context) to see whether batch-size dynamics amplify tails.
- Try hybrid: batch_timeout_ms=6 and max_batch=96 (middle ground).
- Add a run with background cross-tenant noise (15% random extra QPS) to see vulnerability to tenant noise.

Quick decisions / guidance for PRD: for small-to-medium prompt sizes and bursty patterns, prefer shorter batch_timeout (5–6ms) with modest max_batch to reduce tail exposure. But explain cost tradeoff: lower batching reduces per-token efficiency.

Notes-to-self: keep raw CSVs; include trial-level metadata (warm_restart=true/false, kv_hit_rate, gpu_type) in next runs to make bootstrap resampling smarter (stratify by warm vs cold).

Unresolved questions:
- Why did cfgB show occasional >120ms outliers at p99? Hypothesis: background GC on Python worker + large batch recompute; need to correlate system perf samples.
- Is the trial-level bootstrap sufficient or should we do time-window bootstrap (resample windows of 5s) to preserve intra-trial autocorrelation?

Log snippet examples (for trace attachment):
- 2025-02-11T10:02:13.764Z  worker-3  GPU0 context switch: evict 384MB
- 2025-02-11T10:02:13.767Z  worker-3  kvcache miss (key 0x4e3f)
- 2025-02-11T10:02:13.780Z  scheduler   batch-execute size=106 duration=9.8ms

TODO: make a small notebook to visualize bootstrap distributions (violin + CI) and export into PRD slide. Also add a short paragraph on method limits (small-n bootstrap underestimates autocorrelation).

Bottom line (quick): bootstrap from 10 short trials gives directional signal for config ordering and highlights p99 instability; do larger-n confirmation before shipping config recommendations.

-- Marin
